units.text: INT. SELF-STORAGE UNIT 114 - NIGHT
A roll-up metal door, half open, lets in a stripe of sodium-yellow light from the corridor.

The unit is the size of a one-car garage and stuffed to the ceiling: mattresses, a taxidermied heron in a Hawaiian shirt, a canoe, forty identical lamps, a mannequin torso wearing a sash that reads "Miss Tri-County 1987."
ARLO PENROSE-ODUYA (40s, rumpled, a headlamp strapped over a bald head, wet from the rain) ducks under the door and pulls it down to knee height behind him.
He carries a phone, a flashlight, and a bolt cutter.
He looks like a man who has just made a very expensive mistake and is still hoping it is a bargain.
Okay. Okay okay okay.
units.name: ARLO

units.text: He turns slowly, headlamp sweeping the wall of junk.
It lands on the heron.
The heron looks back.
No. No no. You're a lamp. You're clearly a lamp.
units.name: ARLO

units.text: He pokes it with the bolt cutter.
It does not fall over.
He pokes harder.
It falls over.
A cloud of dust erupts, and Arlo coughs, waving a hand in front of his face.
Eighteen hundred dollars. Eighteen hundred dollars for a bird.
units.name: ARLO

units.text: He pulls out the phone, thumbs the screen, and holds it up to his mouth like a man ordering at a drive-through.
Voice memo. Day one. Unit 114.
units.name: ARLO

units.text: He taps the screen.
A small ping.
He lowers the phone, thinks better of it, raises it again.
Contents: one bird. Many lamps. A canoe, which is, I will admit, a promising canoe.
units.name: ARLO

units.text: He climbs over a mattress.
A spring creaks.
The canoe leans toward him.
He catches it with his shoulder, and an avalanche of tennis rackets slides off the top, bouncing around his feet.
Do not panic. Rackets are not a sign.
units.name: ARLO

units.text: He shoves the canoe upright, pats it, and steps toward the back wall.
There, behind the lamps, he spots a steamer trunk wrapped in chain.
He drops to his knees, headlamp bobbing.
There you are.
units.name: ARLO

units.text: He raises the bolt cutter.
The chain snaps with a ringing clang.
He lifts the lid.
Inside: stacks of sealed envelopes, hundreds of them, each stamped with a red wax seal.
He pulls one out and reads the front.
"To be opened upon my death." Okay, that's... that's a lot of deaths.
units.name: ARLO

units.text: He pulls out another.
"To be opened upon my death. Again."
units.name: ARLO

units.text: He sits back on his heels.
Rain drums the roof.
He lifts the phone and presses record.
Update. The bird is not the story.
units.name: ARLO

units.text: He plays back the memo.
His own voice, thin and echoing, fills the unit.
Contents: one bird. Many lamps. A canoe, which is, I will admit, a promising canoe.
units.name: ARLO

units.text: He nods along with himself as though approving a stranger's testimony.
Good. Consistent. Very professional.
units.name: ARLO

units.text: He sets the phone on the trunk and picks up a third envelope.
He turns it over and sees, in blue ink, a handwritten line on the back.
His face changes.
He reads it again, silently, lips moving.
He looks up at the heron.
The heron, on its side, has one glass eye pointed at him.
It's addressed to me.
units.name: ARLO

units.text: He stares at the envelope.
Then, very carefully, he returns it to the trunk, closes the lid, drapes the chain back across it, and sits on top of the whole thing with his hands on his knees.
The rain keeps falling.
We're going to need a bigger unit.
units.name: ARLO

units.text: He picks up the phone and presses record once more.
Voice memo. Day one, continued. Do not buy a canoe. Do not buy a bird. And whatever you do, do not read the mail.
units.name: ARLO

units.text: He stops the recording.
In the silence the phone replays the last line to nobody.
And whatever you do, do not read the mail.
units.name: ARLO

units.text: Arlo reaches slowly for the envelope again.
